Operator
Welcome to the BT Brands Investor Conference Call. Our hosts for today's call are Kenneth Brimmer and Gary Copperud. At this time, all participants will be in a listen-only mode. Later, we will conduct a question-and-answer session. I would now like to turn the call over to our first speaker, Mr. Brimmer, you may begin, sir.
Kenneth W. Brimmer
COO, CFO, Principal Accounting Officer & Chairman
Thanks, Paul. I appreciate the introduction. And with me is also Gary Copperud. So as you have questions when we get to the Q&A, certainly, Gary and I can both address any questions. BT Brands reported after the close today, our 2023 results. And certainly, at first blush and at closer examination in both, they were disappointing. And we were disappointed in the results for the year where we recorded a net loss of $887,368, and that was on $14 million in sales, which was an increase of 15% over the prior year. That increase was largely real because we didn't make any acquisitions during the year. So it was, in general, attributed to the business for the most part that we already owned.
I think when the loss can be a little bit disarming when you see that number. What I'm trying to communicate to everybody today is I think we are more optimistic than ever about what we're going to do with BT Brands. And I think you're going to see some things happen in this next year that are going to reward the patient holders of our shares because we do have at the December 31, 2023, is $6.9 million in cash, and most of that's in treasury bills. And we also have another approximately a little over $1 million of cash under our control at Bagger Dave's. So what I want to try and walk you through today is where we're going to take this company, and what makes it an attractive investment today. I think one of the things, and you guys -- investors can all go through this yourself, but you know when you note the $887 loss, the first thing that sticks out is the equity in our loss in Bagger Dave's, which was $347,000. So that's 35% before tax of our total loss was incurred at Bagger Dave's.
We incurred a nonrecurring expense, although we haven't abandoned our efforts, but we incurred, I guess, an expense of $100,000 if not a little bit more, in terms of legal and other professional services associated with our efforts to inject ourselves on to the board of Noble Roman. So those are two things that are not really in the core operations of Burger Time that both happened last year. And then we're not alone in this as most companies do. We incentivize executives with stock-based compensation and the way the rules are written, you have to attribute a value to those share grants, and that value becomes a charged operations. So we had also a significant charge for stock-based compensation during the year. So all of that said, I'll just go through each of the concepts a little bit briefly. We in Burger Time, we have closed in the last year. Since the end of the year, we closed one of the Sioux Falls stores, and that has, I think, going to be a positive because we've seen the business in the other Sioux Falls store has been up well into the double digits.
So we think we've just moved the customers over to a more efficient model. So we end up with 7 Burger Time locations and 1 DQ franchise. And if you read our filings, which we announced at the end of the last quarter, we are going to exit that Dairy Queen franchise. It really doesn't fit with our business to be an owner of a franchise, to be a franchisee. That's not our approach. It works well for some, but that's not what we're going to try and do. And Dairy Queen has never been completely happy with a public company as a franchisee. They generally are looking for owner operators. So it's been a relationship that doesn't work very well for either of us. So we're working to sell that unit, and that will happen sometime in the next few months. Bagger Dave's, I would call your attention to the Bagger Dave's press release that we issued a couple of months ago. And this is probably the last time you're going to see the name Bagger Dave's, at least in one of our press releases because we plan on changing the name, getting PCAOB audits done, doing a reverse tax split, what level we haven't yet determined. And we are negotiating with several people, because several people have approached us several concepts where they want those Bagger Dave locations.
So how we exactly accomplished that is under negotiation. But what we see, the likely scenario is, Bagger Dave's would actually end up acquiring another concept and convert all 6 Bagger Dave's stores to a new concept, if you will. And one of the things that everybody who's looked at the locations agrees is that, A, the physical plant of each location is in very good shape. The locations are solid. And there isn't any reason that in terms of acquisitions, we've looked at that we couldn't do the system average, if not more. So we're talking about business for whatever reason that's doing, just over $1 million per unit. And we think we can get that up with a better concept and a fresher look. We can get that up to approach of $2 million per unit average unit volume for our 6 units. So now you're talking $12 million in annual revenue. And if we can manage it to kind of an industry standard, you're talking about EBITDA of 15% on that $10 million.
So we're talking going from a losing proposition to our 40% interest being very, very contributory to a positive net income. Pie in the Sky, there's not much to say about Pie. That's been a home run acquisition for us. We paid back our investment in just a little over a year. We are looking at before the town counsel out in Falmouth, Mass. On Monday, we're going to add a liquor license to the concept. We've just seen over our involvement at Pie were in the evening and late afternoon. People are looking for something besides just a croissant or a muffin. So we are going to turn it as the day wears on into a little bit more fuller service. We've got a wonderful outside feeding area right at the ferry terminal, the ferry near to Martha's Vineyard, and it attracts people who would like to sit there and hopefully, we'll end up increasing their check average by consuming beer and wine. So that happens Monday, we expect a favorable outcome there.
Village Bier Garten, transitioning down to Florida, that's still been a challenge for us in terms of getting it to profitability. We've invested a lot in the location to bring it up to what we consider a better standard, but we're still not satisfied. We had one of our employees actually from Pie, who's a chef down there for 10 days, eating the menu, cooking the menu. So we're looking at the menu. We're looking at the basic concept, and I think we're going to be making some dramatic changes there. I skip by Keegan's. Keegan's is our other Florida. It's kind of a traditional Florida fish house. It's in an excellent location across the street from the beach. We benefit from traffic of tourists and locals in the area. And that business, it took us a while to get the kitchen right. As you remember -- some of you will remember, we acquired it from a family who had run it for many years, and they were going to stay and help us with the transition.
Well, we got a little less than full support in terms of that transitional help, and it took us a while to get the staffing right, which relates to food costs, labor costs and a whole bunch of different costs. But we think that's right. And in the last couple of weeks, we've been in the range of $80,000 a week for Keegan's. And that's basically pretty darn close to capacity. We can always do a little a little more at lunch. But I think when we get a week above 80, we're very busy and everybody is making money, including us. So Keegan's is -- we think Keegan's is down the road to recover. So in addition, I guess, the major -- in addition to the major redo of Bagger Dave's, which will be a positive contributor. The other thing that has us very excited is we have the resources to go out. And certainly, we're seeing over the last couple of months, more opportunities than we've ever seen.
And that's what both Gary and I have been focusing on, acquisitions, which -- to make a significant contribution to earnings right now because we understand the importance of delivering earnings for our investors right now, but also things that we have the ability to grow. So our plan for BT Brands is to -- in an ideal world, we would find an acquisition where it had what you might all call proof of concept, where the concept works, retain on investment is high, but it's simple enough and straightforward enough where we could go and roll out 50, 100, 300, 400 units in a major rollout. And obviously, as you take something with proof of concept, you hopefully buy at a low multiple of EBITDA, and can get that monetized in the market at a higher multiple of EBITDA. There's just no question that, that creates a winning formula for the shareholders. And that's what we're focused on right now.
So a disappointing year in terms of financial performance, but we're in a very strong financial position in terms of our ability to look at and do things that are going to be highly accretive to our investors. We're focused on doing the things that are highly accretive to our investors. And I would say, I would look forward to making much more positive reports in terms of earnings in the future. So Paul, with that, we'll take questions that anybody might have.
Operator
[Operator Instructions]. And our first question comes from Roger Lipton of Lipton Financial Services.
Roger Lipton
Lipton Financial Services
Yes, I can. How are you today?
Kenneth W. Brimmer
COO, CFO, Principal Accounting Officer & Chairman
I'm doing well, Roger. Thanks.
Roger Lipton
Lipton Financial Services
Yes. Forgive my voice, we got a little laryngitis. I don't feel as bad as I sound. Regarding Keegan's, $80,000 a week sounds like you did pretty good volume, as you say. But what do you think is realistic in terms of annualized volume there? And what kind of margin is capable of generating?
Kenneth W. Brimmer
COO, CFO, Principal Accounting Officer & Chairman
Yes. So when we originally bought it, the former owners have done a little bit over $3 million in annual volume. Have you been in the store? And it's relatively --
Roger Lipton
Lipton Financial Services
I've seen pictures.
Kenneth W. Brimmer
COO, CFO, Principal Accounting Officer & Chairman
When we get to 80,000, we're really utilizing the capacity at a high level. So what we did, I think this was just smart, and we did it. We add it because you have a lot of groups, families, grandma, grandpa, who come into the store because it's a very family-friendly location. So we added a fair amount of bank at seating along the perimeter inside, which will give us more capacity. I think to answer your question directly, I think we can certainly, in 2024 be at $3.2 million. And I think a bottom line margin, and EBITDA margin would be higher. But I think we're looking at basically a contribution of certainly 10% of that. And we'd like to run the 4-wall contribution at 15% to 20%. And if we get 15 on $3 million, that's a vast improvement from where we are today. And I would say, based on the last month, we're teed up to get to that point. So Keegan's is -- it's a very popular spot. If you go down there and you talk to customers in the store, which I've done. They've been coming there for many years.
There's repeat visits virtually across the board. And we appointed a woman, the General Manager down there, and she's worked in that area for 30 years. She knows the restaurant in and out. And the team at Keegan's is really strong. I mean, they are quality-conscious. The food is excellent coming out. Now, we're not high-end. We're not the fanciest placed on the beach, but this is people who are going out for casual beach dining. But we still -- the average entree is still -- we got the menu right here still well into the high $20s per entree. So we're getting a good check average out of people, and people don't seem to balk at that at all. So we're excited about Keegan's.
Roger Lipton
Lipton Financial Services
As I recall, you had -- you had some competition open there. It affects the situation as well as your own operations.
Kenneth W. Brimmer
COO, CFO, Principal Accounting Officer & Chairman
You know the restaurant business when somebody new opens up, everybody tries them. I would say the competition, we've heard numbers, and it's a very nice door and I ate down there, and they invested probably $4 million plus. But it's still -- it's a sports bar, basically. If you want to go have a grouper sandwich and watch -- which a lot of people do in Florida. So I'm not dissing the sports bar. In fact, we've upgraded our TVs in our place, but it's really much more of a drinking place. As you know, I assume it Keagan's, -- because of our small size, we don't qualify for a full-liquor license under Florida's liquor regulations. So we just have beer and wine. So if you're down there, next time you're in Indian Rock Beach and you want to do tequila shots, you're going to have to go down the street to the competitor and have your needs met there because -- and that's more of their market.
But any time competition comes in, people try it, "Hey, let's try this place." And what we've really stressed this year is excellent customer service because we don't want to -- everybody is going to try it. We just don't want to lose anybody permanently. And at Keegan's, it's just a lovely place and the people are at the front of the house are -- they've been there. Most of them have been there for 20-plus years of servers. And I would tell you, as a group of people, you're not going to find a very professional group of servers. I mean, we're not talking about the college kids and nothing wrong college kids. I've got three of them myself. But you're not going to find them waiting tables. You're going to find servers who are professional, know what they're doing. They're hustling. They take care of the guests and they just have a fantastic attitude. And that makes it a good dining experience. So we all know what it's like to be served by a professional, which doesn't happen everywhere in the restaurant industry today.
Roger Lipton
Lipton Financial Services
So it sounds like Keegan's probably did not make any money in the last 12 months. Is that --?
Kenneth W. Brimmer
COO, CFO, Principal Accounting Officer & Chairman
Well, yes, we have some amortization, some additional amortization, but yes, it was -- had a certainly, EBITDA was around breakeven, but we've -- that's been addressed, I think, aggressively. So that's -- we looked to that. It's got to make a contribution. So that's where we're going.
Roger Lipton
Lipton Financial Services
And how far away from profitability is the Bier Garten?
Kenneth W. Brimmer
COO, CFO, Principal Accounting Officer & Chairman
Well, that's an interesting question. The Bier Garten has to average about -- the breakeven has to average about 30,000 a week. Now, in the last few weeks, of course, it's season in Florida. So we've been above that. So I mean, in the very discrete 1 month, we probably are going to have a profit there. But we've experimented with two things. One is -- and this comes from my staff down there. They talked about -- there's a gentleman who has -- does a show on Friday and Saturday night, and his name is Herb, and he performs over at Disney in Epcot Center, and they're German Pavilion over there. So he's very polished, very professional. And our manager said, "Well, we got to get Herb to come back because that will help build the business.
So Herb is back and he is helping to build the business. So we've got that entertainment product on Friday and Saturday nights, which is going to add to the business. And we've made the menu. We haven't abandoned German food because we know some people come in for -- they come in for a schnitzel or they come in for -- they love our giant pretzel, so they come in to that, and bratwurst and that. But we've added just a very good cheeseburger, and we've added other items that are more in mainstream American that we downplayed the German approach. We still have the German beers, which people do come in for and ask for.
Roger Lipton
Lipton Financial Services
How much did the Bier Garten do under the previous ownership?
Kenneth W. Brimmer
COO, CFO, Principal Accounting Officer & Chairman
Yes, roughly about $1.4 million.
Roger Lipton
Lipton Financial Services
Okay. So not a lot more -- not much more than --
Kenneth W. Brimmer
COO, CFO, Principal Accounting Officer & Chairman
No, not a lot different. And the place was in poor repair when we -- poor repair than we thought. So one could say certainly, we should have improved our -- looking behind the wall, so to speak.
Roger Lipton
Lipton Financial Services
And what are the trends at your 7 Burger Times?
Kenneth W. Brimmer
COO, CFO, Principal Accounting Officer & Chairman
Well, the trends this year in 2024 have been off the charts good. Now, having said that, it's been a function of we had at the beginning of March. We had a very early spring. So we had nice weather everywhere. So our stores were all up double digits through this last week. Now a little last week, the weather kind of regress to the mean, so to speak. So we've had some snow throughout the system in colder weather, which you may have heard this. But we -- it's positive. I think what's hurt us there somewhat is higher labor costs, where as I said in the brief introduction, a few years ago, we could build a staff together and keep them there for maybe $11, $12 an hour, sometimes start people out as low as 9%. Well, now that world doesn't exist anymore.
So you've got -- and then in at least one of our locations, we've had a hard time getting a manager to stick. So we know that if I could take the manager of our best location and clone her, she runs the lowest food cost, the lowest labor cost, and see year-over-year increasing sales by double digits on a base that was our #1 store. So the #1 store, and she's increasing it. So if I could take -- her name is Cecilia. If I could take Cecilia and clone her, and we're going to use her as a resource a little bit more because she does a lot of things right. But I think what happens is she just runs the store with a lot of intensity, which you are familiar with a lot of fast-food concepts, and I was in one of the major competitors right here in Minneapolis, a national chain with a very large market value. And I would tell you, their service had zero intensity. So getting a manager, as we've said, even from the time we went public in these burger type stores who can really take ownership and can run it with passion is the key. And we've had some of those, and we have some that aren't. And certainly, in one of the locations this past year, we got her profitability-wise by management turnover, I think we went through to managers. And it takes a while to figure out.
Roger Lipton
Lipton Financial Services
You said the double-digit sales increase this year up until the last week or so. Was that a function of weather or what? Because --
Kenneth W. Brimmer
COO, CFO, Principal Accounting Officer & Chairman
Weather was a part of it. Yes. Weather was a part of it because, I mean, literally, we had -- although the high day is going to be here in a minute time where I am, there's going to be 18. We had -- we've already had a couple of days in the '70s, so -- and the snow was all gone. So it became -- it just really became an early spring, which certainly helped. And then we went through the cycle where we obviously did extremely well during COVID, and our business was up 30%, 40%. And then slowly, it kind of regressed to what one could assume were pre-pandemic levels. But I think now, I think that was -- the bottom has been established and now we're going to bounce off of that, hopefully, significantly.
Roger Lipton
Lipton Financial Services
All right. That's -- I don't want to dominate any further. Thank you, Ken.
Kenneth W. Brimmer
COO, CFO, Principal Accounting Officer & Chairman
Okay. Thank you, Roger.
Operator
Thank you. [Operator Instructions]. And seeing no further questions, I'll turn the call back over to our host.
Kenneth W. Brimmer
COO, CFO, Principal Accounting Officer & Chairman
I think we're good. Well, we appreciate the patience of our shareholders, and we appreciate the support of our shareholders. And the way we show our appreciation is to deliver results. And that's definitely our focus right now. So thanks, everybody, for joining us on today's call, and we look forward to talking with you at the end of the third quarter, which -- at the end of the first quarter which ends on Sunday. So that comes up pretty fast. Thanks, Paul. Appreciate it. Log us off.
Operator
The meeting has now concluded. Thank you for joining, and have a pleasant day.
Kenneth W. Brimmer
COO, CFO, Principal Accounting Officer & Chairman
Great. Thank you.

content.text:
Operator
Welcome to the BT Brands Q2 2023 Earnings Call. Our host for today's call is Kenneth Brimmer. [Operator Instructions]
I would now like to turn the call over to your host, Kenneth Brimmer. You may begin.
Kenneth W. Brimmer
COO, CFO, Principal Accounting Officer & Chairman
Thank you, Jen, and welcome to everybody on the call today -- on the BT Brands call. With me today is our CEO, Gary Copperud. And I think Gary will have some remarks towards the end of this call, but we're looking forward to discussing the quarter with you.
And before we dig into that, I'm going to at least call everybody cautionary attention that we, no doubt, will be making some forward-looking statements today. And as you're all well aware, these are not historical facts and no assurance of future performance is assured. Therefore, we caution you all not to rely on any forward-looking statements that we may make today.
Our quarter for BT Brands, as many restaurants are, we're on a 4-4-5 accounting period. So each accounting period is 13 weeks. So the quarter ended on July 2. And if you go to the press release, I'm not going to reread all of the tabular information that's in that press release. But we did have a bottom line after-tax benefit loss of $375,000. And I would say, it goes without saying that it was a disappointing quarter in terms of that performance and it's performance that we are aggressively addressing right now.
I would go back and say -- call everybody's attention, I think, for [indiscernible], we are certainly a bit of a balance sheet story. We ended the quarter basically with around $7 million in cash and marketable securities, and that excludes another approximately $1.5 million that is sitting in Bagger Dave's, which we own 42% of that. And that is really essentially unchanged from the end of the first quarter. So even though we have a significant loss, it really wasn't a big consumer of cash during the quarter. And simple math will show everybody that, that $7 million in cash is a little more than $1 a share in cash and certainly, our priority is to put that money to work in a prudent fashion. And obviously, as we get it to work and generate more revenue and hopefully, bottom line profit, we're going to be able to leverage some of the G&A costs, which also impacts us.
We -- if you look at the tabular numbers, we run around 13% G&A right now, and that's really too high. We need to get the business growing to the point where that's much more down in the below 7% range and closer to 5%. So that's the long-term goal in terms of growing this business. We have the good cash to grow the business. And those of you who have taken a few minutes to study our 10-Q and our balance sheet are certainly well aware we've got a modest amount of long-term debt, a very low percentage of our $10 million in equity with roughly $2.5 million found in the current portion of debt. And we were obviously either lucky or very smart to have refinanced the mortgages on the Burger Time stores before interest rates started to move up with long-term permanent financing at 3.45%.
So we've got a very strong financial position. We're in a very strong position to go implement the business plan, which is to look at acquisitions and we're pursuing things all the time. Obviously, most of them don't come to fruition for one reason or another. And we usually tell people at the front end of any of the negotiations that we're aggressive buyers, and we're -- we have the ability to close quickly, which is our main benefit, but we combine that ability with hopefully not paying top dollars or anything.
So a couple of comments on the quarter, and I think you're probably hearing this from other restaurants. Certainly, we have seen a slowing of the rapid inflation that we saw last year. It's moderated and it's actually really benefiting us right now at Pie in the Sky, our $3 million coffee shop out in Woods Hole, Massachusetts. Because I think egg and butter, certainly eggs are less than half the price they were a year ago. And obviously, in baking, you use a lot of butter and that's down somewhat significantly from a year ago as well.
So we've seen a lowering of commodity prices, which are benefiting us out there in terms of probably right now a couple of hundred basis point pickup in the bottom line operating profit percentage of that business. So that is performing very well.
And in terms of the other big thing that restaurants like to talk about, the labor markets, we've seen the labor market, I would say, at all of our locations, somewhat more stable. It's not that we have got loads of surplus employees. And obviously, for some of the seasonal -- more seasonal places like Pie in the Sky, we're still actively hiring as kids go back to college and we need to tap up through the fall.
But we have -- we're not struggling as we were last year, if you recall our conversation certainly at our Burger Time in Minnesota, North Dakota, South Dakota. We had weeks and days where we actually had to curtail hours, either close at 6 or close on a Sunday, where we, very simply, at least as the managers reported did not have the employees to fully staff. That doesn't exist right now. I'm told, as of today at Pie where we keep open, even though we're a coffee shop, we stay open in general in season until 11:00 at night to service people coming in and out of the ferry terminal. And it does create some challenges in cleaning the store.
And basically, as the significant portion of our labor force is going back to college, I understand this week, we're going to close at 9:00, which is not a material impact on the business. However, we'll certainly close the sandwich -- we grow our own sandwiches out there, breakfast sandwiches of that style and that will close at 9:00.
So in terms of some of those basic components of the restaurant business, that's kind of our term report. When we turn for a minute to Florida, which is we have 2 restaurants down there, Keegan's Seafood Grille and the Village Bier Garten. Both of those performed in a disappointing manner, and I would say, there's obviously some depreciation and amortization on both of those locations. But certainly, where we thought we would have an operating profit through the 6 months of somewhere well in excess even after depreciation of $100,000, we were in the area of losing that amount of money at the operating level after depreciation and amortization.
So we are in the process of digging through all of the details in terms of where our menu pricing is at, where our commodity costs are at, where our labor costs are at. And I would say, you can certainly hold us accountable as we get on the next call. So break this one down. We're very aggressively turning with -- turning to get Keegan's on back where we thought we bought it.
The Village Bier Garten is a little bit of a different animal. It's a large open space. I'm going to assume nobody has been there, but it's a traditional German -- if you were to go to Germany, it's what you might see in a beer garden, a lot of outdoor picnic tables, which give us a lot of capacity. And I can only report what our team has told me. And obviously, I look at the weather every day for all of our locations because like any retailer, whether it does impact the business somewhat positively and somewhat negatively.
So our team in Cocoa, Florida where the Bier Garten is located certainly points to the weather this year as having some fluctuations that have hurt business now. What impact that's had, we're going to also have to figure out.
And then turning to -- just rounding the horn at Pie in the Sky is performing better than last year and certainly better than our expectation. That's offset a little bit by the Burger Time business, which came out of the pandemic with really unbelievably strong numbers. And it bases the competition of fast food. Now we've been able to maintain margins in the face of some rising beef costs there. And in general, we've kept our menu costs. As those of you who are familiar with the history of Burger Time, we tend to want to be a value provider. We try and be in terms of our competition, priced just a little bit lower than anybody else, and we've maintained that.
We'll probably be looking at a price increase here as we go into the fall because our competitors certainly have been very aggressive in increasing prices. I want to just talk for a minute as we get to the bottom of the income statement. We pick up our equity portion, our equity in Bagger Dave's. Here as most of you are aware, we own 41.2% of Bagger Dave's and that has been, again, the loss, but the loss is, for the most part, cash -- noncash loss, it's depreciation. It's -- and our equity in the loss certainly made up a significant portion. If you look at the 26-week numbers, at the 6-month numbers, we had the loss of $375,000, which I talked about at the beginning of the call and $145,000 that before the tax benefit related to our equity share in the Bagger Dave's loss.
So that's also, if you want to line up our priorities aside from the number one priority, aggressing debt in the capital that we have in a way that generates a return that is acceptable and that's a high return. And number two is fixing Florida, which we are aggressively working at pursuing steps in both of those locations to improve results. And then number three is, and this is -- a big priority is to really look at the Bagger Dave's business, which is principally over in Michigan, also in Indiana and Ohio.
But we -- our goal there as those stores are -- and we've had a lot of, I would say, friends, people in the restaurant industry who maybe have ideas for us, probably 4 different groups go over and tour the 6 Bagger Dave's stores and the reports have been consistent as to be: a, the locations are pretty good. Some are better than others. But generally, the locations are decent. The properties are in like new condition. They're in very good shape. They're not run down. And the staffs are -- in the restaurants are all reasonably good in terms of the interaction that people had with them.
Now the problem with Bagger is -- as we've assessed it, is really a problem with the concept. So we're in the process of pursuing some other concept, and we've looked at and discussed internally several different alternatives. My own view is that we could change it to almost anything, and we would probably get a 30%, 40% increase in sales. And those of you who are quick with a calculator, if you take those 6 stores and multiply it by even a reasonable sales effort, which would be an average of $1.5 million. And certainly, we have the capacity to do over 2 million in all those locations. But let's just say the 6x $1.5 million is $9 million, and that's -- we're able to generate 15% and it's patch-sheltered that drops to the bottom line in those locations. That's a pretty significant impact on BT Brands' financials and obviously, we'll be building cash that we could put to work inside of Bagger Dave's.
So that's -- again, we've sort of been talking to people and considering things. But I think we're -- as we get in the second half of the year, we're going to take some aggressive steps to reposition all of those locations with something that is newer and more exciting in terms of the consumers' desire to try what we're doing and to participate as a regular customer.
So that actually, I'm pretty excited about because I think that solves the problem, both at BT and obviously allows us to build cash in the Bagger Dave's public company, which we own 41.2% of that. So that's kind of a rundown of where we're at. And I think, hopefully -- obviously, we're in a very enviable strong financial position. We've got the ability to move forward and do take advantage of opportunities. I mean, certainly, when you look at Florida, where we put the -- our toe in the water, we've got some stores that are not doing what we'd like to see, but it's also not killing us. It's not going to put us out of business. We're obviously going to be able to weather the storm as our cash stays roughly the same, and we look for a way to put that to work.
We also know that with interest rates up, we're going to probably see a second half unless we find an opportunity to take advantage of some higher interest income on our available cash balance. So with that -- I know there's going to be probably some questions on our interest in Noble Roman's, which is included in our investments and the proxy fight that we went through, and I'm not going to bore you with all the details as to why our votes got excluded.
We did collect significantly more proxy than Noble did, although we were not allowed to nominate Gary Copperud to the Board, which was our desire because we hoped that Gary would be a catalyst for change. And I guess, from our standpoint, and I'm going to let Gary add words on that, as we have said in the press in Indianapolis and have said to publicly regarding our investment in Noble Roman's, although things could change any time. Certainly, it's -- our current intention is not to go away. We're going to stay with it. That's our plan. And we think we have the opportunity next year to perhaps elect multiple directors and to definitely influence the outcome of our investment.
So Gary, do you want to add anything on the Noble side before we throw it open to questions.
Gary W. Copperud
CEO & Director
Well, just commenting on it a little bit is that we are only running for 1 out of 5 board seats. And so we didn't plan really on any significant changes other than holding the directors accountable for their actions in which they've continued to dilute the existing shareholders with employee stock options, which mainly went to the insider executives that are already overcompensated. And at the end of the day, is that over a 10-year period, they've diluted the existing shareholders by up to 23% of the outstanding shares. And they're all approved by -- or not getting them approved by outstanding shareholders. So that was pretty significant in addition to their older compensation.
That being said is that we have the ability to fix what their problems are. And the main problem is really twofold. One is the overcompensation of what management takes out for a large portion of their years and not fully disclosing what that full compensation is. And the other is that just their user rates on which they're borrowing money at in which we feel that we can get bank financing with and paring back their $1.6 million of interest costs at 15% round numbers is that we have the ability to change that.
What is significant only from the standpoint is that we made an investment in the company of, I don't know, $0.5 million, plus or minus, which is not big in relationship to our liquidity that we do have on our books, but we have significant ways in order to lower that cost significantly. And we anticipated that it was probably going to run over 2 elections before we got much done from a board level because the independent board members are just not acting as fiduciaries to the outside shareholders is basically rubber stamping to the existing management that they've done for a number of years.
So at the next election, because there wasn't a quorum is that there's going to be 3 out of the 5 board seats, that will be up for election, and we plan on being there doing what we did this year next year as well. And anything can change from all kinds of different things with these -- with the characters that are currently involved in. But -- and we look forward to significantly having an impact when we do have 3 Board members on it next year, assuming that we have the same 75% of the existing shareholders that vote for us.
The company did state in their 8-K that they had 9 million shares that voted for them, in which, on our tabulation is that the 2 officers that are also Board members ended up voting their 3 million shares and plus or minus another 0.5 million shares by the Board of Directors that voted for them. So on the tabulations that we have is that we feel that they probably ended up getting 4 million votes, and we ended up getting roughly about 10 million shares because pretty much the existing shareholders have seen over the years, the 90% decrease in stock price and the decline in shareholder equity has gone -- 50% of it or 40% of it has gone to the insiders to no benefit of the existing shareholders.
So how they can give out all of the stock options each and every year and the compensation that they give these -- the people, we think that it's way outside of the box of being normal. So other than that, I think we can open it up for questions.
Kenneth W. Brimmer
COO, CFO, Principal Accounting Officer & Chairman
Go ahead, Jen. You can see if there are any questions out there.
Operator
[Operator Instructions]
Mr. Brimmer, there are no questions at this time.
Gary W. Copperud
CEO & Director
I would say a quick -- a couple of more quick closing the loop is that one of the things that Kenneth talked about is, is that the $3 million or $2.5 million that we have on debt is against the real estate at roughly about 50% of what the appraisal value was. So our debt is tied with what we've had a fair amount of appreciation on our real estate. And that was fixed cost of about 4.5% for 10 years is what we've got mortgages on -- that's the only debt that we've got with the company.
Kenneth W. Brimmer
COO, CFO, Principal Accounting Officer & Chairman
Okay. Gary and I are both available, I think our phone numbers are easy to find, if you have a question following this call or want to follow up on specific items. But again, we appreciate everybody joining us today. We appreciate your interest in BT Brands.
Gary W. Copperud
CEO & Director
Ken -- and I think there's one more comment that both Ken and I are almost shocked about is that -- I mean, we went into Noble as a shareholder because we saw value there. And what is significant to us is that in spite of us reaching out and willing to lend them some money to pay down that debt is that we have yet to get a simple phone call on how we can help them when we're -- when we have the ability to -- in order to do it. So that was the other significant thing, I think that really shocked and surprised us is that nobody from the company has ever reached out to us.
Kenneth W. Brimmer
COO, CFO, Principal Accounting Officer & Chairman
Okay. All right. I think we are just through. Jen, thank you for hosting, and thank everybody for joining, and we look forward to speaking with you and being held accountable to those priorities as we head to the end of the third quarter. So thank you for joining us.
Gary W. Copperud
CEO & Director
Thank you.
Operator
This does conclude today's conference call. Thank you for attending.
